nameStory: Tall Beggarticks gets its name from two distinctive features: its impressive height (often towering over other wetland plants) and its 'begging' seeds. The achenes (dry fruits) have two sharp, barbed prongs that grab onto clothing, fur, and anything else that brushes past, as if begging for a ride to new territory.
description: Tall Beggarticks is an annual wildflower that's like the lanky teenager of the wetland world. This hairy-stemmed plant typically grows 1-2 feet tall but can shoot up to over 3 feet when conditions are right. Its small yellow flowers look like tiny sunflowers with short, stubby petals, and it produces those infamous hitchhiker seeds that seem to find every hiker's socks and shoelaces.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, wedge-shaped seeds with two sharp, backward-pointing barbs that feel like tiny fishhooks when you try to remove them from clothing

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flower heads with bright yellow centers and 3-5 short yellow petals that are only a few millimeters long; some flower heads have no petals at all

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves made up of several lance-shaped leaflets, each up to 3 inches long, arranged opposite each other on the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright annual with a noticeably hairy stem that feels rough to the touch and branches toward the top where flowers cluster

habitat: Look for Tall Beggarticks in wet, muddy places throughout New England's lowlands. You'll find it thriving along stream banks, pond edges, marshes, swamps, and even roadside ditches that stay moist. It loves rich, mucky soil and often grows alongside other moisture-loving plants like jewelweed and wild mint.

seasonality.spring: Young seedlings emerge in late spring with their first simple leaves, before developing the characteristic compound leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and begin flowering in mid to late summer, producing their small yellow blooms from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and become hitchhiker hazards from late August through October, when the barbed achenes are at their stickiest and most annoying.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist through early winter, but the annual plant dies back completely, leaving only seeds to sprout next year.

funFact: The barbed seeds of Tall Beggarticks are so effective at hitchhiking that they inspired the invention of Velcro! Swiss engineer George de Mestral studied how these and similar burr-type seeds stuck to his dog's fur and his own clothing after nature walks.
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with other beggarticks species, but Tall Beggarticks lives up to its name by being noticeably taller than most of its relatives. Remember: if it's growing in water and you can barely see the flowers over the other wetland plants, it's probably the 'tall' one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Devil's Beggarticks' by some, this plant isn't particularly devilish - that common name is more often used for its relative Bidens frondosa. The 'devil' association comes from the frustratingly persistent seeds that seem impossible to remove once they've grabbed hold of your clothes.
compareHints: Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems. Devil's Beggarticks is typically shorter with smoother stems, while Nodding Beggarticks has flower heads that droop downward. Water Marigold has much more feathery, underwater leaves and larger, showier flowers with longer petals.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
